CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR                           §

    JG & WILSON SISTERS RANCH, LTD.’S REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ BRIEF ON
                PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

        COMES NOW Intervenor JG & Wilson Sisters Ranch, Ltd. (“Wilson Sisters Ranch”) in

the above-styled case, and pursuant to the deadline set by the Commission, files Reply to the Brief

of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(“Applicants”) on Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 11 and 13 filed on October 7, 2026, 1 and

respectfully shows as follows:

                                INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

        Wilson Sisters Ranch files this Reply to reiterate to the Commission that the Administrative

Law Judges’ (“ALJs”) recommendation to deny the Application remains fully supported by the

record and the Applicant’s answers to Issues 11 and 13 do not justify the Certificate of




1
  Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13, PUC Docket No. 59475, Item No. 59475-6623 SOAH
Docket No. 473-26-16349 (Oct. 7, 2026).
 Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) approval. 2

           The Applicants attempt to circumvent the evidentiary record by asserting that ERCOT’s

Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) alone mandates approval, despite the ALJs’ explicit

findings that the Applicants failed to prove project need under PURA Section 37.056 and

committed notice violations by denying approximately 1,400 landowners their statutory right to

pre-filing public meetings. 3 Because the Applicants’ load forecasts collapsed under scrutiny—

relying heavily on unverified officer letters resting on an unverified S&P Global study whose

methodology the ALJs found deeply flawed—the Application must be denied.

                                             REPLY TO APPLICANTS’ BRIEF

PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11: RELIABILITY STANDARDS

      The Applicants failed to meet their evidentiary burden under PURA Section 37.056 and
16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II)
           The central pillar of the Applicants’ brief is the repetitive assertion that ERCOT’s Permian

Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) and Regional Transmission Plans (RTPs) must be accorded “great

weight.” 4 This argument selectively truncates the Commission’s own procedural rule. Commission

Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) does not grant blind, automatic deference to ERCOT planning

documents. The rule contains an explicit statutory condition precedent:

           “The forecasted load growth and additional load currently seeking interconnection must be

           substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth.” 5


2
 See SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum, PUC Docket No. 59475, Item No. 59475-6441 SOAH Docket
No. 473-26-16349 (Aug. 20, 2026); see also Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1.
3
  Compare Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 11 (“There is simply no evidence in the record to overturn ERCOT’s
three separate intendent recommendations…”), with SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 92 (finding that
“the greater weight of the credible evidence is against the recommendation” and that the PBRP load forecasts were
unsubstantiated).
4
    Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 11.
5
    16 TEX. ADMIN. CODE § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II).




                                                       2
 Additionally, the ALJs examined the underlying record in the August 20th Proposal For Decision

(“PFD”) and found that the PBRP load forecasts were overstated, unsubstantiated, and plagued by

material errors. 6 Specifically, 11,695 MW of the modeled demand by 2030 consisted of

speculative, non-binding, non-oil-and-gas commercial expressions of interest—primarily

uncommitted cryptocurrency mining operations, speculative data centers, and unfinanced

hydrogen facilities. 7

            Rather, the actual, quantifiable load trends since the adoption of the PBRP demonstrate

that load growth has materialized at levels significantly below the modeled forecasts, and the

composition of large industrial interconnection requests across Texas has shifted substantially. 8

Because the Applicants’ load figures failed to provide the quantifiable verification mandated by

Rule 25.101, the ALJs correctly held that the PBRP recommendation cannot be accepted by the

Commission for Import Path 2.

            Ultimately, the Applicants’ demand for “great weight” deference ignores the reality of the

PFD. The ALJs explicitly accommodated the Applicants’ preferred standard, noting that even if

they afforded great weight to ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation, the evidentiary presentation was

so fundamentally flawed that it collapsed anyway. 9 In fact, the ALJs found that the record evidence


6

Global’s methodology” and finding the study’s projected forecasts “overstated and outdated”); see also id. at 92
(concluding that ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation “is not ‘substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load
growth’”); see also id. at 178 (Finding of Fact No. 108) (formalizing the finding that the forecast are “overstated and
outdated”); see id. at 181 (Finding of Fact No. 138) (formalizing the finding that the recommendation is not
“substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth”).
7
 Id. at 61–62 (noting that the 11,695 MW of non-oil and gas demand was heavily composed of crypto mining (59%),
green hydrogen (22%), and data centers (6%), with only 39% confirmed by contract); see also id. at 173 (Findings of
Fact Nos. 75–76).
8
  See id. at 63–64 (highlighting the Commission’s 2025 finding that “recent actual experience” showed “previously
forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt level[s] than initially claimed”); id. at 75 (noting the material
“shift in relative share” system-wide between crypto and data center load); see also id. at 175, 176 (Findings of Fact
Nos. 89, 95).
9
    Id. at 92.




                                                           3
 actively defeated the presumption. As the ALJs concluded, even starting with that highly

deferential presumption, “the greater weight of the credible evidence is against the

recommendation.” 10 The Applicants did not fail because the ALJs refused to give ERCOT

deference; they failed because an unverified forecast cannot trigger an irrebuttable presumption of

need, and their evidence simply could not meet the burden of proof.

           The Fallacy of the “All-or-Nothing” Integrated PBRP Defense
           The Applicants argue that because ERCOT studied the PBRP as a single integrated package

and modeled all three 765-kV lines together under NERC TPL-001-5.1 contingencies, SOAH and

the Commission are legally prohibited from removing any component from the plan without an

“independent power-flow study” showing the remaining pieces still resolve system violations.11

However, ERCOT’s methodological choice to bundle these projects for its internal studies does

not rewrite Texas law, nor does it shift the burden of performing independent modeling onto the

Commission or protesting landowners. Realistically, the Applicants simply fail to prove granular,

independent need. A CCN proceeding evaluates a specific utility application to condemn land and

construct specific facilities under PURA Section 37.056. The Applicants bear the burden of

proving that this specific line is necessary. 12

           Under cross-examination, Applicants’ witness Gurley admitted that ERCOT never

performed an isolated power-flow study evaluating whether the system would remain reliable with


10
     Id.
11
   Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 10–11 (arguing that the PBRP is an “integrated reliability plan,” that ERCOT
“studied the paths together” to satisfy NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, and that the record does not support
“the ad hoc removal of any component” without an “independent analysis or planning study” showing the remaining
system resolves the violations).
12
  See SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 15 (“Applicants bear the burden to prove . . . that their requested
CCN amendment is necessary” under PURA § 37.056); id. at 89 (agreeing that the evidentiary record must
demonstrate the PURA § 37.056 factors support the specific line “as a line that stands on its own”); see also id. at 99
(concluding that “Applicants had to show Import Path 2 is independently necessary under the PURA § 37.056 factors.
They did not.”).




                                                          4
 only Import Paths 1 and 3 in service. 13 ERCOT’s failure to run sensitivity models excluding Import

Path 2 is a structural evidentiary omission by the Applicants, not a shield to prevent regulatory

scrutiny. The absence of line-specific modeling means the record lacks granular evidence proving

that Import Path 2 itself cures an independent NERC violation.

            Ultimately, the Applicants cannot use their own failure to conduct an isolated power-flow

study as a legal loophole to bypass the rigorous, facility-specific statutory requirements of PURA

Section 37.056. As the ALJs correctly recognized, NERC contingencies that influence ERCOT’s

overarching regional planning “are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import

Path 2.” 14 Since the Applicants failed to present a case for the need of Import Path 2 separate and

apart from the comprehensive multi-line project, they fundamentally failed to meet their burden of

proof, compelling the denial of the Application. 15

            The Far West Texas GTCs Do Not Validate Import Path 2

            The Applicants attempt to sidestep their defective PBRP forecasts by claiming that

ERCOT’s September 2025 Far West Texas Import Generic Transmission Constraints (“GTCs”)

create an urgent, operational reliability crisis that requires Import Path 2. 16 Notably, not only were

the GTCs never part of the PBRP approved by the Commission in Docket No. 55718, but although

ERCOT designated the GTCs in September 2025, the Applicants withheld this theory from their

direct case. Instead, they introduced it only through rebuttal testimony on May 28, 2026—a mere




13
  Id. at 88 (noting Mr. Gurley admitted “Applicants had not performed a partial build study to justify Import Path 2
individually”).
14
     Id. at 89; see also id. at 180 (Finding of Fact No. 130).
15
  See id. at 99 (concluding “Applicants did not present a case for the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from
the three 765-kV import paths as one comprehensive project”); see also id. at 180 (Finding of Fact No. 129).
16
   See Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 7–8 (arguing that the Far West Texas Import GTCs are designated as IROLs
under NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4 and present a “tangible threat to reliability” requiring Import Path 2).




                                                                 5
 two weeks before the hearing on the merits. 17

           Procedural defects aside, the Applicants have simply provided no cure for their deeply

flawed load projections. As the ALJs correctly recognized in the PFD, GTCs merely measure

transmission system constraints; they do not validate the composition or reliability of the

speculative load on the demand side. 18 Because the Applicants failed to disaggregate the load

driving the GTC from the speculative data center and crypto load undermining the PBRP, this late-

filed operational theory does nothing to cure the fundamental defect in the underlying baseline

load forecasts.

           Furthermore, Import Path 2 is not the exclusive solution to these grid constraints. As

established by the Applicants’ own witness Collin Martin, Import Path 2 is merely one of seven

transmission upgrades and exit strategies evaluated by ERCOT to address the GTCs. 19 It cannot

serve as a post-hoc justification for a multi-billion-dollar 765-kV infrastructure project when the

baseline demand drivers supposedly necessitating the project remain entirely unsubstantiated.

           The Distinguishable Precedents of Import Paths 1 and 3

           The Applicants argue that the Commission’s approval of Import Path 1 and Import Path 3

compels approval of Import Path 2 because they stem from the same PBRP. 20 In the proceedings

for Import Paths 1 and 3, the presiding ALJs recommended approval based on the specific

evidentiary records developed in those cases.


17
     SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 82.
18
     Id. at 83; see also id. at 179 (Finding of Fact No. 114–116).
19
  See Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at Exhibit A, p. 12 (quoting Applicants’ Ex. 14, Martin Reb. at 16, which admits
ERCOT identified six transmission projects to resolve the North-Far West GTC and eight transmission projects to
resolve the South-Far West GTC); see also SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 83 (noting the 765-kV paths
are merely “one of seven transmission upgrades ERCOT asserts as ‘help’ to exit the GTCs”); id. at 179 (Finding of
Fact No. 113).
20
  See Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 10–11 (noting the Commission’s approval of Import Paths 1 and 3 on the
basis of the PBRP and arguing “[t]here is no valid reason to reach a different conclusion for Import Path 2”).




                                                             6
            However, the Commission’s prior approvals in separate dockets do not operate as a rubber

stamp for every line associated with the PBRP. In contrast to those prior proceedings, the ALJs

conducted an exhaustive review of the evidentiary record here and concluded that the Applicants

failed to substantiate public need. 21 Rather than binding the ALJs to approve Import Path 2, the

severe deficiencies and speculative load assumptions exposed in this record call into question the

premise of the PBRP itself, highlighting that regional over-building must stop where the

evidentiary foundation collapses. 22

PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 13: RELIABILITY STANDARDS

           Seeking Economic Credit Without Economic Scrutiny

           The Applicants take an inconsistent position on Issue 13. They admit that under

Commission Rule Section 25.101(b)(3)(A), Import Path 2 is framed strictly as a reliability project

and is legally exempt from the formal economic criteria, consumer cost tests, and production cost

tests required for economic projects. 23 Yet, they spend the entirety of their Issue 13 briefing

reciting unvetted, high-level economic figures, asking the ALJs to make positive Findings of Fact

regarding consumer cost savings. 24

           Realistically, the Applicants cannot have it both ways. By exempting themselves from the

rigorous economic project framework, they avoided submitting their models to standard market




21
  See SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 1, 98–99 (concluding, after an exhaustive hearing, that the
Applicants failed to show the PBRP’s underlying projected loads establish a need and failed to establish that Import
Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public).
22
  See, e.g., SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 81 (finding the PBRP’s baseline S&P Global study built its
projections on “surveys of unconstrained ‘wish list’ scenarios and corporate pledges—speculative and unconfirmed
load” resulting in “overstated and outdated” forecasts); see also id. at 92 (finding the recommendation “is not
‘substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth’”).
23
     Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 16.
24
   See id. at 18–19 (requesting the ALJs issue findings of fact on consumer savings and avoided construction costs
despite the exemption).




                                                         7
 simulation benchmarks, product-cost vetting, and direct discovery by opposing parties. Unverified

economic claims imported from high-level ERCOT whitepapers cannot be transformed into formal

administrative findings of fact. As the ALJs correctly concluded, because this is exclusively a

reliability project, “the estimated cost of the facilitates to consumers, and congestion-cost-savings

analysis are not required,” and “the record contains no evidence quantifying either.” 25

           The Capital Cost vs. Savings Imbalance

           Even if these unverified economic claims are considered, they fail basic economic scrutiny

when balanced against the actual project costs. The Applicants point to generic estimates of

approximately $229 million in annual consumer energy cost savings and $28 million in annual

production cost savings compared to a 345-kV alternative. 26 ERCOT’s own comparative studies

in the record show that the 765-kV strategic expansion plan carries an astronomical total cost

estimate of $23.91 billion, compared to $20.98 billion for the 345-kV alternative, representing an

incremental capital cost premium of nearly $3 billion. 27

           An annual production cost savings of $28 million does not provide economic justification

for a multi-billion-dollar capital expenditure premium. Texas consumers will ultimately pay for

the return on equity, carrying costs, and depreciation of this capital buildout through their

transmission cost of service (TCOS) rates, wiping out any projected consumer savings. In fact, as

the ALJs noted, the Applicants failed to provide the estimated cost of the facilitates to consumers,

submitting only the projected construction capital costs while leaving massive financial variables–

–such as tariff exposure on steel and aluminum––completely unanalyzed. 28


25
     SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 150; see also id. at 191 (Findings of Fact Nos. 225, 227).
26
     Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 18–19.
27
  See Applicants’ Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 (2024 Regional Transmission Plan) at 22 (showing the estimated cost
of the 345-kV plan is $20.98 billion, compared to $23.91 billion for the 765-kV plan).
28
     SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 149.




                                                           8
          Deconstructing the “Bidirectional Flow” Narrative

         In an attempt to further bolster these unverified economic benefits, the Applicants try to

rebrand the lines as serving a dual economic purpose. They claim they will operate

“bidirectionally” to alleviate congestion and export cheap, curtailment-prone West Texas wind and

solar to eastern demand centers. 29 Yet, the core engineering design of the PBRP import paths is

explicitly built around importing bulk power westward into the Permian Basin during periods of

low local wind generation. 30

         The Applicants fail to grasp the difference between curtailed renewables and speculative

siting. Simply put, the record does not substantiate that 765-kV transmission lines routed through

Bell, Big Hill, and Sand Lake are the most efficient means to unlock renewable exports. Instead,

the bidirectional claim masks the reality that the lines are being built to import power to subsidize

speculative, localized industrial operations (such as uncommitted data centers and crypto miners),

rather than delivering verifiable net savings to residential and small commercial consumers across

the ERCOT footprint. 31 Furthermore, the Applicants’ narrative collapses entirely upon the ALJs’

finding that neither Oncor nor ERCOT performed the studies necessary to prove there is even

sufficient central Texas generation available to simultaneously serve local data-center load and

export power westward via Import Path 2. 32

                                                 CONCLUSION


29
  See Applicants’ Brief, supra note 1 at 8, 17 (arguing the projects will operate bidirectionally to alleviate congestion
and export renewable energy).
30
  SOAH Proposal for Decision, supra note 2 at 84 (quoting the PBRP’s statement that “significant amounts of the
regional transmission upgrades will be needed to transfer power to the Permian Basin region”); id. (noting
Commission Staff witness Poole confirmed the PBRP’s justification “was not bidirectional”).
31
  See id. at 61, 74–75 (finding that 65% of the projected non-oil and gas load is made up of crypto and data center
load).
32
   See id. at 86 (noting Applicants admit no determination was made regarding whether central Texas generation is
sufficient to serve both functions).




                                                           9
        For the reasons detailed in this Reply, Wilson Sisters Ranch respectfully requests that the

Commission overrule the Exceptions of the Applicants and Staff, adopt the Proposal for Decision,

and deny the Application in its entirety. The record clearly demonstrates that Import Path 2 is not

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, nor is it supported by verified economic

benefit.

          Deconstructing the "Bidirectional Flow" Narrative

         In an attempt to further bolster these unverified economic benefits, the Applicants try to

rebrand the lines as serving a dual economic purpose. They claim they will operate

"bidirectionally" to alleviate congestion and export cheap, curtailment-prone West Texas wind and

solar to eastern demand centers. 29 Yet, the core engineering design of the PBRP import paths is

explicitly built around importing bulk power westward into the Permian Basin during periods of

low local wind generation. 30

         The Applicants fail to grasp the difference between curtailed renewables and speculative

siting. Simply put, the record does not substantiate that 765-kV transmission lines routed through

Bell, Big Hill, and Sand Lake are the most efficient means to unlock renewable exports. Instead,

the bidirectional claim masks the reality that the lines are being built to import power to subsidize

speculative, localized industrial operations (such as uncommitted data centers and crypto miners),

rather than delivering verifiable net savings to residential and small commercial consumers across

the ERCOT footprint.31 Furthermore, the Applicants' narrative collapses entirely upon the ALJs'

finding that neither Oncor nor ERCOT performed the studies necessary to prove there is even

sufficient central Texas generation available to simultaneously serve local data-center load and

export power westward via Import Path 2.32
